name: Indian Lake
lede: Indian lake is an old name for a red lake pigment made from lac, the resin of an Asian scale insect; as a screen color it is a dull, greyish purplish red.

sections.title: A pigment named for its source
sections.body:
Indian lake is a name for the red made from lac, the encrusted secretion of insects, and the "Indian" refers to where those insects lived [1][2]. Treating the word as one fixed recipe would be a mistake: the terms for insect-based reds were often applied indiscriminately, so lac, cochineal and kermes were muddled together [2].

In a lake pigment the dye is precipitated onto a mineral base, and with careful control of acidity a lac lake could be pushed from orange through red to violet [3]. A nineteenth-century writer quoted in the Pigment Compendium called Indian lake rich, transparent and deep [1].

sections.title: Lac in Europe
sections.body:
Lac reached Europe around 1220 and became the main red lake of the Renaissance; so much of it was used that the word "lake" came to cover red dye pigments in general [3]. It turns up in paintings by Lippi, Ghirlandaio, Michelangelo, Tintoretto, Holbein and de Champaigne, from about 1475 to 1637 [2].

Its weakness was fading: lac is described as having poor lightfastness, though it survives as a food and cosmetic colorant [3]. Winsor & Newton still listed lac in 1896, but by about 1898 the maker Reeves said it used alizarin instead [1].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch is the Ridgway 1912 and ISCC-NBS 1955 color of that name, a greyish purplish red, and the Maerz and Paul dictionary dates the name in English to about 1250 [4]. It is a standard-system color, not a measurement of any pigment, so a real lac lake could differ from it [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In the ColorHub archive this color matches 23 paintings, about 0.1% of the 23,531 we hold, as photographed [5]. A match is rare, which fits a color that sits between the brighter reds and the dark browns.
